Again, let [MATH: \Phi(t)] be a fundamental matrix for the linear system
[MATH: \mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x},]
where [MATH: A] is an [MATH: n\times n] matrix. The fundamental matrices have the following important properties.

sections.normalized_html:
1. Satisfies the underlying system. Indeed, since each column of [MATH: \Phi(t)] is a solution of the system, we have [MATH: \Phi'(t) = A\,\Phi(t).]

  2. Invertibility. The columns of [MATH: \Phi(t)] are linearly independent for all [MATH: t,] so [MATH: \det\Phi(t)\neq 0] for all [MATH: t.] In particular, [MATH: \Phi(t)] is invertible for all [MATH: t.]

  4. Non-uniqueness. If [MATH: C] is any invertible constant matrix, then [MATH: \Psi(t)=\Phi(t)\,C] is also a fundamental matrix for the same system.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider the homogeneous linear system
[MATH: \mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x},]
where [MATH: A] is an [MATH: n\times n] matrix.

Content:
A fundamental matrix for this system is an [MATH: n\times n] matrix [MATH: \Phi(t)] whose columns are [MATH: n] linearly independent solutions of the system.

Content:
If [MATH: \mathbf{x}_1(t),\dots,\mathbf{x}_n(t)] are linearly independent solutions, then one fundamental matrix is
[MATH: \Phi(t)=\big[\mathbf{x}_1(t),\dots,\mathbf{x}_n(t)\big].]

Content:
Note: The columns of [MATH: \Phi(t)] can be written in any order.

Content:
Let's see an example.

---

Item 2 — Example: Constructing a Fundamental Matrix

Example Prompt:
[MATH: [5|1; 0|5]]
Consider the system of linear ODEs and two of its linearly independent solutions [MATH: \mathbf x_1] and [MATH: \mathbf x_2,] shown above. Find the fundamental matrix for the system.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Given a linear system [MATH: \mathbf{x}' = A \mathbf{x},] where [MATH: A] is an [MATH: n \times n] matrix, a fundamental matrix [MATH: \Phi(t)] of the system is an [MATH: n \times n] matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our cases, we have a [MATH: 2 \times 2] system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

[MATH: x_{1}(t)|= [4; 0]e^{5t} = [4e^{5t}; 0]; x_{2}(t)|= [4t; 4]e^{5t} = [4te^{5t}; 4e^{5t}]]

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as
[MATH: [4e^{5t}|4te^{5t}; 0|4e^{5t}]]

Note: The columns of [MATH: \Phi] can be written in any order.

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: Properties of the Fundamental Matrix

Content:
Again, let [MATH: \Phi(t)] be a fundamental matrix for the linear system
[MATH: \mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x},]
where [MATH: A] is an [MATH: n\times n] matrix. The fundamental matrices have the following important properties.

Content:
1. Satisfies the underlying system. Indeed, since each column of [MATH: \Phi(t)] is a solution of the system, we have
[MATH: \Phi'(t) = A\,\Phi(t).]
2. Invertibility. The columns of [MATH: \Phi(t)] are linearly independent for all [MATH: t,] so
[MATH: \det\Phi(t)\neq 0]
for all [MATH: t.] In particular, [MATH: \Phi(t)] is invertible for all [MATH: t.]
3. Representation of solutions. Every solution [MATH: \mathbf{x}(t)] of the system can be written in the form
[MATH: \mathbf{x}(t)=\Phi(t)\,\mathbf{c},]
where [MATH: \mathbf{c}] is a constant vector.
4. Non-uniqueness. If [MATH: C] is any invertible constant matrix, then
[MATH: \Psi(t)=\Phi(t)\,C]
is also a fundamental matrix for the same system.

Content:
We'll now get some practice.

---

A derivation showing that [MATH: \Phi(t)] satisfies the matrix differential equation [MATH: \Phi'(t) = A \, \Phi(t)] is given below.
